guides.title: Addiction and Recovery: A Bible Study on the Long Road Back
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on bondage, confession, relapse, and grace, for people in recovery and the families who love them.
guides.blurb:
This study is for people who can't stop drinking or using and wish they could, for people in recovery who know how fragile the ground can feel, and for the spouses, parents, children, and friends who love someone caught and have run out of ways to help. It is also for the small groups and church recovery ministries that gather around them. Its five sessions move from the divided will of Romans 7, through hiding and confession, relapse and the long wait, and the father who runs in Luke 15, to the new life Galatians sets before people who have been set free. Each session is built so a busy volunteer can lead it without preparing a lesson; the leader's primer is the one thing to read beforehand. Every question comes with a note for the leader on what it is after, and every session ends in prayer.

This guide is a companion to treatment and to recovery communities, never a substitute for them. It is not a recovery program, and it does not replace a doctor, a licensed counselor, a treatment program, or the people who walk with someone day by day. Stopping alcohol and some other drugs suddenly can be medically dangerous, so anyone who drinks or uses every day should stop with a doctor's help. An overdose is a 911 emergency. The leader's primer says what to do when someone in the room is in danger.

The study takes two common answers seriously. One says addiction is a choice, and the cure is repentance and a better choice; the other says it is a disease of the brain, and the cure is treatment. Each holds part of the truth, and Scripture will not let either have the whole. Paul describes a man who is both responsible and held captive, and who finds his rescue in a person rather than a technique. The study also refuses to let anyone lead it from above. Many who lead or attend a study like this have never had a body that depended on a drink or a pill, but nearly everyone knows the divided will in some smaller form, the promise to stop that did not hold, and that is enough to take away anyone's right to look down on anyone else. The church has failed people caught in addiction with contempt and with silence, and those who lead this study stand inside that failure.
guides.audience: People in recovery, families who love someone caught, church recovery ministries, and small groups

guides.title: Advent: A Bible Study on Waiting for the Light
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study for the four Sundays of Advent and Christmas, on a people in the dark, the comfort of a long-promised God, Mary's song, the Word made flesh, and the Christ who will come again.
guides.blurb:
This study is for churches and small groups keeping the four weeks before Christmas, and for anyone for whom December is the hardest month of the year. Its five sessions, one for each Sunday of Advent and one for Christmas, read Isaiah's promise of light to a people under Assyria; God's comfort for exiles in Isaiah 40 and old Simeon's long wait; Mary's yes and her song, in which God brings down the proud and lifts the humble; John's confession, with the Nicene Creed, that the Word became flesh; and the hope of Christ's coming again, for everyone who carries an empty chair into Christmas. Each session is built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question comes with a note on what lies behind it, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This study won't hurry anyone to the manger. Advent waits on purpose, and its waiting is a mercy to the people December's cheer leaves out: the grieving, the lonely, the newly divorced, the poor, and the estranged. It reads Isaiah in his own century before reading him toward Christ, because the promises were first spoken to people in real darkness and are stronger for it. It names the questions faithful Christians still disagree about, and it leaves them open. And it implicates its writer and its leaders, who have also trusted the protections they could see, grown impatient with long waits, and heard Mary's song as good news about someone else's fall. It begins where Advent begins, in the dark, where the promise was first given.
guides.audience: Churches and small groups keeping Advent, households, and anyone for whom December is the hardest month
guides.sessionsLabel: 5 sessions (through Advent, or as 8 or 4 weeks)

guides.title: After Christendom: A Study on Post-Christian Faith
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on following Jesus faithfully in a world that no longer pretends to be Christian.
guides.blurb:
This study is for Christians who can feel the ground moving, for pastors who aren't sure what their church is for anymore, and for small groups willing to look at the present as it is instead of mourning a past that was never as Christian as we remember. Its five sessions ask what has actually ended and why that may be a mercy; how Jeremiah taught the captives in Babylon to live; how the church bore witness before it had any power; what it means to be a creative minority instead of a defeated one; and what hope looks like when it stops looking backward. A volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question comes with a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer.

It won't tell the church to fight harder to win back a culture that has moved on, and it won't hold a funeral either. Panic and denial are the two easy roads, and both are dead ends. Cultural Christianity is ending. But the end of Christendom isn't the end of the church. The church started on the far side of Christendom, small and strange and without a single law on its side, and it turned the Roman world upside down. We built more on the culture than on Christ than we'd like to admit, and this study starts there.
guides.audience: Thoughtful Christians, pastors, and small groups in a secular age

guides.title: Aging and Legacy: A Bible Study on Finishing Well
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on aging, death, and the life that outlasts you.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has started to feel time move differently: the person watching a parent decline, the one who has buried a friend, the one who no longer looks young in the mirror, and the small groups that carry them. Many of us have sat in churches that talk about heaven and almost never about dying. These five sessions talk about dying. The first reads the plain arithmetic of Psalm 90 and the gift of a limit. The second sets the culture's fear of aging beside the Bible's honor for gray hair, without pretending the losses of age aren't real. The third faces death as the last enemy and the One who defeated it. The fourth asks what legacy really is. The fifth is about finishing the race in the company of the saints. A leader, even a grieving one, can run it with no preparation. Every question comes with a note, and every session ends in prayer.

This study won't stand above death and explain it away, and it won't hurry anyone to glory before the loss has been mourned. It will never hand a grieving or frightened person a slogan in place of a Savior. Where someone is drowning in grief, facing a diagnosis, or sinking toward despair, it says plainly that the ache is real, that "The LORD is near to the brokenhearted" (Psalm 34:18), and that there's help worth reaching for. The resurrection isn't a reason to skip the valley. It's the reason you can walk through it.
guides.audience: Older adults, caregivers, the grieving, and any small group willing to face mortality

guides.title: Alone in a Crowded Church: A Study on Church Loneliness
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on loneliness, belonging, and the community Christ actually promised.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has stood in a full sanctuary, sung every word, shaken every hand at the door, and driven home knowing that no one in that building could have told you what was wrong. It's for small groups, adult classes, and church leaders who built the programs and can't understand why the people in them are still so alone. Its five sessions look at the difference between attending and belonging, the shared life the first believers practiced in Acts, the friendship the church has quietly let die, the "one another" commands of the New Testament, and the slow work of being known. A volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question comes with a note, and every session ends in prayer.

It won't scold lonely people for not trying harder to plug in. The harder truth is that the church often produces the loneliness it laments. We built buildings you can hide in. We mistook a crowd for a body and attendance for love. We made the coffee hour a place where everyone reports that they're fine. Pastors can lead hundreds of people and still feel unknown in their own congregations. Most of us have asked "How are you?" without waiting for the answer. This study starts there, with all of us inside it.
guides.audience: Anyone who has felt alone in church, small groups, and church leaders

guides.title: Anger: A Bible Study on Temper and Righteous Anger
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on anger, its roots, and the God who is slow to it.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has scared themselves with their own temper, and for the small groups that carry them. Many of us were taught anger one of two ways: as a sin to repent of the moment you feel it, or as a right to defend. These five sessions try to say what anger actually is. The first treats anger as a signal rather than a verdict. The second sets Jesus in the temple beside Jonah on his hill to tell righteous anger from the self-righteous kind. The third digs under anger to the fear, grief, and wounded pride that usually feed it. The fourth looks at the God who calls himself "slow to anger." The fifth treats forgiveness as the long release of a debt. Anyone can lead it with no preparation. Every question comes with a note, and every session ends in prayer.

Most of us have called our temper honesty, nursed a grievance until it became a wall, or let contempt stand in for a grief we wouldn't feel. This study doesn't stand above that. And it will never tell someone that their anger at a real harm done to them is proof of their own failure. Where someone has been wronged, the anger is often the truest thing in the room. Anger is a fire. It can warm a house or burn it down, and the difference is the hand that holds it.
guides.audience: Anyone who struggles with anger, and small groups working through it together

guides.title: Anxiety: A Bible Study on Worry and the Peace of Christ
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on anxiety, and the peace Christ gives instead.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult classes, and anyone tired of being told to stop worrying by people who have never lain awake at three in the morning doing the math on a life that won't balance. Its five sessions ask what anxiety is and isn't; why Jesus told us to look at the birds and the lilies; what Paul meant by peace, writing from a prison cell; what it means to cast our anxieties on God "because he cares for you"; and the rest Christ offers people who are tired in a way sleep doesn't touch. A volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question comes with a note, and every session ends in prayer.

This study won't tell anxious people their faith would fix them if it were stronger. Some anxiety is the soul reaching for the wrong refuge, and the gospel speaks to that with power. Some anxiety is a body that has stopped working as it should, or a grief that hasn't finished, and that needs a doctor and is no more a sin than a broken arm. The study holds both, and won't make the second sound like the first. Most of us have lain awake, gripped the wheel the whole way home after a sermon on peace, and called our dread discernment. We start there.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Attention: A Bible Study on Technology and Distraction
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on attention, the phone, and the slow recovery of a present life with God and the people in front of you.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has picked up a phone to check one thing and looked up an hour later having checked nothing that mattered. It's for the person who can't sit in a quiet room without reaching for it, the parent who has read a bedtime story with one eye on a screen, the Christian who can't pray for five minutes without the urge to scroll, and the pastor watching a congregation grow more anxious and less present every year. It's also for the skeptic who suspects, rightly, that something is being done to all of us and isn't sure the church has anything to say about it.

It won't hand anyone a productivity system or a thirty-day cleanse with a finish line, and it asks the leader to refuse those too. Attention isn't a resource to optimize. It's the stuff a life is made of and the form love takes, and a soul that can't attend can't love God or anyone else well, however much it wants to. The five sessions move from what the feed is quietly making us into, through the research on the phone-based childhood taken at its strongest and tested against Scripture, to the old practices of Sabbath and silence, the slow reading of Scripture against the scroll, and finally a rule of life for an actual household. I don't write this as someone who has beaten the machine. Nobody leading it should pretend to have, either.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Baptism and Communion: A Bible Study on the Sacraments
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on baptism and the Lord's Supper, on why God gives his people physical signs, and on the water and the meal that mark and feed the church.
guides.blurb:
This study is for new believers, baptism and membership classes, small groups, and any Christian who has passed through the water and taken the bread for years without stopping to ask what they are. Its five sessions ask why Christianity, unlike a philosophy, insists on things you can touch; what to make of the long disagreement between churches that baptize believers and churches that baptize the infant children of believers; what baptism says about who a Christian now is, buried and raised with Christ; how faithful Christians have understood what happens at the Lord's table; and why the meal was given to make a divided people one. A volunteer with no seminary training can lead it. Every question comes with a note for the leader, and every contested point is stated in its strongest form before any verdict.

The study doesn't pretend the differences are small, and it doesn't treat them as walls. I say plainly where I land on baptism and on the table, and I still try to state the other views so fairly that a thoughtful believer on the other side would finish feeling understood rather than beaten. What the study won't do is let a disagreement about the timing of a baptism or the way Christ is present at the Supper divide the one body he died to make one. These questions are worth studying and deciding. They were never worth breaking the table over.
guides.audience: New believers, membership and baptism classes, and small groups of any tradition

guides.title: Believe: A Bible Study for New Believers and Seekers
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on what Christians actually believe, and why it is both reasonable and life-giving.
guides.blurb:
This study is for new believers taking their first steps, for seekers circling the faith with real questions, and for small groups willing to slow down and ask what the gospel is before anyone is asked to sign on to it. Drawn from my book Believe, its five sessions ask whether there is a God at all and what kind; who Jesus claimed to be and why the claim can't be sidestepped; whether he actually rose from the tomb; what faith and doubt really are; and what it costs, and gives, to follow him. A busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question comes with a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer rather than in winning an argument.

The study doesn't treat doubt as the enemy or seekers as projects to be closed, and the leader shouldn't either. Faith isn't the absence of questions, and a faith that has never been tested isn't strong, only untested. Some objections to Christianity are weak and fall apart on their own. Others are serious and have been asked by the church's best minds for two thousand years, and those deserve a real answer, not a slogan. The study tries to hold both.
guides.audience: New believers, seekers, small groups, and adult Sunday school

guides.title: Biblical Womanhood: A Bible Study on Women of Valor
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on womanhood, calling, and the image of God.
guides.blurb:
This study is for women who have wondered whether the church actually believes what Genesis says about them, for the men who have quietly assumed it was written for them, and for the small groups willing to read the whole canon instead of the same three verses. It walks slowly through five sessions, beginning with the dignity Genesis 1 gives every woman as the image of God and the way the fall distorted that dignity into rivalry and rule. It recovers the women the church forgot to teach, Deborah who judged Israel, Huldah who authenticated the word of God, Junia counted among the apostles, Phoebe who carried the letter to the Romans, Priscilla who corrected a preacher, Mary Magdalene sent to tell the men that Christ was alive. It takes the eshet chayil of Proverbs 31 back from the checklist it became and returns her to what the Hebrew says, a woman of valor, a warrior word. It reads the hard texts, First Timothy 2 and First Corinthians 14, and sets the complementarian and egalitarian readings side by side, each in its strongest form, before it lands. And it ends on calling in every season, single, married, mother, widow, worker, refusing to reduce a woman's worth to any one of them.

This is not a study written down to women from a safe height. It is written by a man, a pastor, the father of five sons, who has to confess at the outset that men built much of the church for men, that its sermons have often quoted Paul's hard sentences to women and skipped the women Paul honored by name, that men in pulpits have taught rooms as if half of them were furniture. He writes from inside that failure, not above it. And on the contested questions of what women may do in the church, the study refuses the cheap win in either direction. It states the complementarian case and the egalitarian case each the way its own best defenders would state it, sorts the matter honestly by how much it binds, and names where the author lands and the strongest objection he has not fully answered. A woman on the other side of that question should finish feeling understood, not beaten. The dignity is not up for a vote. The rest is held with an open hand.
guides.audience: Women, the men who worship beside them, and mixed or women's small groups

guides.title: Character Before Competence: A Church Leadership Study
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on leading the church without losing your soul.
guides.blurb:
This study is for pastors, elders, deacons, and the teams who carry a church together. It's also for anyone who has felt the distance between the person the work demands and the person they actually are. Over five sessions it looks at what God actually screens for in a leader, at the inner life and the exhaustion nobody sees, at the idol of being needed, at who you put in the room and why nobody is safe to lead alone, and at the three things that have brought down most of the leaders we've lost, along with the last work of raising the person who comes after you. A busy leadership team can run it with little preparation. Every question carries a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer rather than strategy.

It isn't a study that lets the gifted off the hook because the numbers are good, and it isn't a study that looks down on skill. Someone who can't teach shouldn't be appointed to teach, and a treasurer who can't read a balance sheet is a liability, however willing. The argument is about order. Character is the foundation and competence is the house built on it. I'm not writing from outside this. Leaders like me run the searches that let a bright gift do the screening character should have done, handle holy things all week without being fed by them, and build ministries that can't run without us. Those are my dangers too, and the study asks every leader at the table to read it as a mirror.
guides.audience: Pastors, elders, deacons, and leadership teams

guides.title: Christian Nationalism: A Five-Session Bible Study
guides.eyebrow: A pastoral five-session study on what Christian nationalism is and isn't, for people on every side of it, that keeps the cross above the flag.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult classes, and anyone tired of a phrase that gets thrown like a rock in two directions and wants to know what it actually names. It works through five of my essays. It defines Christian nationalism without slandering the man whose grandfather landed at Normandy, and it confronts the fusion of nation and faith without sneering at ordinary believers who love their country. A busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer rather than argument.

It isn't a study that flatters one party and scolds the other. It asks the conservative whether he has married his country to God and won't let anyone question the marriage. It asks the progressive whether he fears religion in public only when it's the wrong religion, and whether he has put his own hope in the state. And it asks the same of me. I'm not writing from outside this temptation, and neither is anyone who leads it.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Contentment: A Bible Study on Wanting Less
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on contentment, envy, and the restless heart.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has most of what they once prayed for and still wakes at three in the morning wanting more, and for the small groups willing to sit with them in it. Over five sessions it looks at the restless heart and the culture of more, at envy and the comparison that spoils a good gift, at the secret Paul said he had to learn, at the strange accounting of godliness with contentment, and at the Sabbath heart that trusts the God who sent bread one morning at a time. It turns down two easy answers: the prosperity teaching that says God wants you to have more, and the grim piety that treats every desire as sin. A tired volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer.

I'm not writing this from a shelf above the wanting. Most of us have refreshed the same screen looking for a number that would make us feel like enough, said congratulations with our mouths while something soured in our chests, and told God we trusted him for tomorrow while quietly stocking up against it. I have. The one place this study won't go is to shame anyone for a real need or a real grief. Contentment isn't pretending nothing is wrong, and it isn't a command to be fine while the roof leaks or the diagnosis stands. It's a rest you learn, in the God who is enough underneath the things that aren't, and there's room here for the person whose want is hunger rather than greed, with a path to real help kept in view.
guides.audience: Anyone wrestling with restlessness, envy, or the ache of more, and the small groups that carry them

guides.title: Deconstruction: A Bible Study for When Your Faith Comes Apart
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on faith deconstruction, handled pastorally, for the person taking an inherited faith apart to see what's actually true.
guides.blurb:
This study is for the person pulling a faith apart piece by piece, for the friends and pastors who love them and don't know what to say, and for small groups willing to sit with hard questions without panicking. Over five sessions it asks what you're actually taking apart when you say you're deconstructing, whether doubt is a sin, what to do when the church itself is the reason, how to rebuild on rock rather than on rubble, and what a faith looks like that's small enough to be true and strong enough to hold weight. A busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer rather than a conclusion.

It won't try to talk anyone out of their questions, and the leader must never let it become that. Deconstruction isn't betrayal, and it isn't a fad. It's what a thinking person does when the answers they were handed stop carrying weight. Many people taking their faith apart aren't leaving Jesus. They're leaving a version of him somebody sold them, and telling those two departures apart is what this study is for. Some of what comes down deserves to: the cultural baggage, the borrowed certainty, the politics dressed as the gospel. Some of it is a load-bearing wall, and the cost of pulling it out only shows later. The study holds both. It won't make faithful sifting sound like abandonment, or make abandonment sound like courage. And I don't stand outside this. I'm a pastor, and pastors like me did the bundling, wrapping God and the institution and the politics into one package and handing it over as if it were all the same thing.
guides.audience: Those deconstructing, their friends and pastors, and small groups

guides.title: Deep Roots: A Bible Study on the Basics of the Faith
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the doctrines we recite without using, the church we forgot we owe, and the single story Scripture has been telling all along.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and anyone whose faith has outgrown the slogans it was handed and who suspects there's more under the floor than they've been shown. Over five sessions it looks at the gospel as news rather than advice, and the God who turns out to be three; at whether a copied and contested Bible can still be trusted; at the fracture in the human heart, the costly grace that meets it, and the God-man who paid; at the councils, creeds and Reformation the church fought through so we wouldn't have to lose the gospel and find it again from scratch; and at the one story the whole Bible tells, and the strange overlap of the ages we live in now. A busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer.

It won't let the lifelong churchgoer recite the creed like a museum label, and it won't treat the skeptic as a fool for asking whether any of it happened. Each session takes the hardest form of the objection first and says what's true in it before answering, because a faith that can't survive the strongest version of the question was never deep enough to stand on. And I'm not teaching this from a safe distance. Preachers like me have preached the ladder and called it grace, prayed to a lonely idol while confessing the Trinity, used the Bible as a weapon, and kept the ledger we say Christ has torn up.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Divorce and Blended Families: A Bible Study for Starting Over
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on grief, Scripture, children, stepfamilies, and the church, for people walking through divorce, the remarried, and the families and churches that love them.
guides.blurb:
This study is for people whose marriages have ended or are ending, for the remarried, for stepparents and stepchildren of any age, and for the churches that love them, or ought to. Its five sessions take up the grief and shame of a marriage's end, read alongside Malachi 2 and Psalm 34; what Jesus and Paul taught about divorce and remarriage, with the three main Christian views stated as their own defenders would; the children caught in the middle; the slow work of a blended family, read through Ruth and Naomi; and the church as family for people whose families have broken. Each session is built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation, and each ends in prayer rather than advice.

Safety comes first throughout. Scripture never requires anyone to stay in danger, and no one should be counseled to return to it; the leader's primer says what to do if someone discloses abuse, danger, or thoughts of suicide. This guide is not legal advice or counseling. Divorce, custody, and support law vary by state, and the study points people to lawyers, advocates, and licensed counselors for what a small group can't give.

The study refuses the two answers churches have often given divorced people: a verdict, with a verse quoted in the lobby and a quiet removal from the places they served, and a silence, with friends who disappear and ministries built as though every family were intact. Each alone tells a divorced person there is no place for them anymore. The study holds the lifelong intent of marriage and the dignity of divorced people together, leaves open what faithful churches answer differently, and implicates the writer and the leader with everyone else. Most of us have broken faith in smaller ways, and many of us have been the friend who went quiet.
guides.audience: People walking through divorce, remarried couples, stepparents and stepchildren, and the churches that love them

guides.title: Doubt: A Bible Study for When Faith Has Questions
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on doubt, deconstruction, and the God who isn't afraid of either.
guides.blurb:
This study is for the believer whose faith has started asking questions the church taught them not to ask, for the small group that wants to talk about doubt without anyone reaching for the panic button, and for the skeptic who came along to be heard rather than fixed. It walks slowly through the hardest questions faith faces: suffering that doesn't resolve, a God who seems to hide, a Bible whose reliability is contested, a church that did real damage, the doctrine of hell, and the supposed war with science. Each question gets stated at its strongest before anyone answers it, because a faith that has to misquote the objection to survive it isn't worth keeping.

It won't shame the doubter, and it won't flatter him either. It draws one careful line. There's doubt that is faith asking God a hard question while refusing to let go of his sleeve, the doubt of the father who cried, "I believe; help my unbelief!" (Mark 9:24). And there's a kind of deconstruction that has already decided to leave and is only narrating the exit. The study treats both with more respect than people expect. It won't pretend the person leaving has no reasons, and it won't pretend anyone is in danger of hell for asking. It ends where Job and Thomas ended, with a faith that has been through the fire rather than one that never asked.
guides.audience: Skeptics, Christians with questions, small groups, and individuals

guides.title: Evangelism: A Bible Study on Sharing Your Faith
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on telling the truth about Jesus the way a witness tells the truth, not the way a salesman closes a deal.
guides.blurb:
This study is for the ordinary Christian who has quietly decided that evangelism is for other people. For the one who flinches when the word comes up, who has watched the bad versions of it and wanted nothing to do with them, who loves Jesus and would still rather do almost anything than bring his name up at the dinner table. It is also for the seeker and the skeptic in the room, the friend who has been handled before and would like, just once, to be met instead. It walks slowly through what it actually means to speak of Jesus without a script, one movement at a time. Why we dread it, and which fears are wisdom and which are caricature. What a witness is, against the salesman who closes and the arguer who wins. The life lived together that makes the question askable before a word is ever said. The telling of your own story, honest about the doubt and the cost, not packaged into a tidy before-and-after. And the long patience of friendship and God's own timing, evangelism as a table you keep setting rather than a decision you pressure.

This is not a study that will hand anyone a technique. It will refuse that on purpose, because the technique is most of what went wrong. Witness is not a sales process and a person is not a target, and the moment we treat them as one we have already lost the thing we were sent to give. Bell does not stand outside the dread. He came to faith from atheism, and he takes seriously how evangelism feels from the other side of the table, where many skeptics have been treated as a project to be closed rather than a person to be known. He is not standing over this study explaining evangelism to the reluctant. He is one of them. Most of us have frozen at the table, said nothing when we should have spoken and said too much when we should have listened. He writes from inside the fear, and the leader will lead from there too.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Faith and Politics: A Bible Study on the Church and Political Power
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on nationalism, empire, and the cost of a free church.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult classes, and anyone who has watched the church reach for the kingdoms of this world on the world's terms and call the reach faithfulness. It moves through five sessions. We start on the mountain where Jesus was offered every kingdom for one bent knee and said no. Then we try to name Christian nationalism carefully, on the right and on the left. We look at the long marriage of church and empire that began under Constantine, at the coin they brought Jesus to trap him, and at what it costs a church to say, and mean, that Jesus is Lord and Caesar is not. Every question comes with a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer rather than a political verdict.

This isn't a study about politics, and you'll need to say so more than once, because almost everyone who walks in will assume it is. It's a study about the cross and about who the church belongs to. It won't tell anyone how to vote, and it won't let either side sit comfortably while the other gets named. I don't write it from outside the problem. I've wanted the shortcut, excused my own side, and kept loyalties I swore weren't loyalties. I'm writing toward a free church, not from one, and I'm asking you to lead it the same way.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Faith on Monday: A Bible Study on Living One Whole Life
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on following Jesus through an ordinary week.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who were handed a faith for Sundays and a calendar for the other six days, and who have lived in the gap between them so long they mistook the gap for adulthood. It walks slowly through five movements drawn from James Bell's book The Undivided Life, on the life lived in boxes and the one life offered whole, on marriage as covenant and the home that forms us, on the refusal to rest and the limits of the body, on all honest work as a calling, and on the rival god of money and the wholeness that is the real standard of a life. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This is not a study about doing more. It is a study about being one person. The divided man is exhausted in a way he cannot explain to his doctor, because he is running several incompatible lives on the same set of bones, preaching generosity and hoarding, counseling patience and raging in traffic, believing God holds the future and lying awake managing it. The gospel offers, before it offers anything else, the rejoining of the man, one life surrendered to one Lord who is finally allowed to walk down the hallway and turn on the lights in the rooms we kept dark. And it implicates the leader and the writer first. Bell does not stand outside this. He came to faith from atheism, and he has lived in the boxes. Most of us have, confusing output with worth, refusing rest and calling it devotion, serving the rival god and building a fortress called security. He writes from inside the dividing. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Fatherhood: A Bible Study for Men Without a Blueprint
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the father wound, the father heart of God, and the long work of raising children who outlast you
guides.blurb:
This study is for the man who is trying to father well from a blueprint he was never handed. Maybe your own father was absent, or present and cold, or there and then gone. Maybe he was good and you still feel the weight of doing for your children what was done for you. We begin where most men begin, in the ache, and we move from the ache to the only Father whose love does not depend on your performance, and from there to the daily, unglamorous work of presence, discipline, blessing, and handing down a faith you have not finished learning yourself. It is written for fathers, for the men who will become them, and for the church that has too often handed men a job description instead of a gospel. No session asks you to pretend you have arrived. Every session assumes you are still in it.

The man writing this is not standing outside the subject explaining it. He was raised without a father. He came to God out of atheism, and he is now raising five sons of his own, fathering forward into a gap. Many fathers have corrected a child in anger they regretted before the words were finished, traded presence for provision and called it love, and waited for a word of blessing that never came. He writes from inside the wound he is asking you to name, and the leader will lead from there too, because nothing in this study works from above. It only works shoulder to shoulder, one unfinished father next to another.
guides.audience: Fathers, fathers-to-be, men's groups, mentors, and any believer carrying a father wound
guides.sessionsLabel: 5 sessions (run as 5 weeks, a weekend retreat, or 10 shorter meetings)

guides.title: Forgiveness: A Bible Study on the Hardest Word
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on forgiveness, what it costs, and the freedom on the far side of it.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who have been told to forgive by people who have never been hurt the way they have been hurt. It walks slowly through five movements on what forgiveness is and is not, on the debt we could never repay and the servant who would not forgive a fraction of what he had been forgiven, on releasing a person who never said sorry and never will, on the false choice between mercy and accountability, and on the slow obedience of forgiving when the wound does not close and the one you most need to forgive is God or yourself. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with zero preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This is not a study that tells wounded people their pain would lift if they just let it go. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. Forgiveness is not forgetting, not excusing, not pretending the wrong was smaller than it was. It is the costly decision to release a debt that is real, to absorb a loss that someone else caused and will not repay. To forget the wrong too soon is to side with the wrongdoer against the victim. Miroslav Volf, who wrote Exclusion and Embrace from inside the wreckage of the Balkans, would not let forgiveness become a demand that the wounded forget; whatever final forgetting there is, he placed at the end, as God's gift in the world to come, not as a duty laid on the injured now. The study holds the cost and the freedom together and refuses to make either cheap. Most of all it implicates the leader and the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He was raised without a father, and he does not stand above the long work of forgiving. Most of us have held a grudge and called it standing for justice. He writes from inside that struggle, not above it. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Friendship: A Bible Study on the Love We Forgot
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on friendship, loneliness, and the covenant of companions.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has more contacts than they have ever had and fewer friends than they can admit, and for the small groups willing to say so out loud. It walks slowly through five sessions on the love the modern world quietly demoted, on the loneliness that followed and the friendship C.S. Lewis said we stopped naming, on the covenant of David and Jonathan who bound their souls together in a court that wanted one of them dead, on the friend who wounds faithfully when a flatterer would have kept the peace, on the strange thing Jesus said the night before he died when he called his followers friends, and on the ordinary work of keeping a friendship alive in a mobile, distracted, exhausted age. It is built so a busy person or a volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer rather than in the ache people already carried into the room.

This is not a study that stands above friendship and dispenses advice about it. The writer came to faith from atheism and was raised without a father, and he does not point from a safe distance. Most of us have been the friend who let the friendship starve because we were busy, who kept the acquaintance and lost the brother, who confused being surrounded with being known. He writes from inside the indictment. So will you. And the study will not pretend that friendship is a small thing you get to when the important loves are handled. Scripture calls friendship a love strong enough to knit two souls, faithful enough to wound, costly enough that the Son of God gave his life for his friends and then, astonishingly, called us that. We forgot it was a love at all. This study is the work of remembering.
guides.audience: Anyone carrying loneliness, and the small groups that meet honestly

guides.title: Generosity: A Bible Study on Giving
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on generosity, contentment, and the heart that gives.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has quietly noticed that their fist is tighter than they wish it were, and for small groups willing to look at money the way Scripture does, as a matter of the heart before it's a matter of the budget. Its five sessions look at the open hand as a spiritual matter before a financial one; at the widow's two coins and the accounting God actually keeps; at contentment as the soil generosity grows in; at hospitality and the table, where generosity gives far more than money; and at cheerful giving as the freedom of someone who has stopped believing he owns his own life.

It isn't a study about tithing percentages or a household spreadsheet, and it isn't about fixing an economy. It's about the grip, the one you can't feel until you try to open it. It's built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries notes on what it's after, and every session ends in prayer rather than in the guilt people already carried through the door.

Most of us have called our tightfistedness stewardship, given the round number that cost us nothing and felt generous doing it, and lain awake counting on a security that was never going to save us. I have. So the one thing this study won't do is turn the open hand into a new law to fail, a heavier weight on people already crushed, or the lever prosperity teachers use to promise that God will repay your giving with interest. Generosity doesn't buy blessing. It's what a freed hand does, the shape a heart takes once it has believed it was given everything.
guides.audience: Individuals, couples, and small groups

guides.title: Gratitude: A Bible Study on Thanksgiving and Grace
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on gratitude, grace, and the eucharistic heart.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone tired of gratitude taught as a life hack: a mood to manufacture, a journal you keep until the good feelings come. It's for people who want to know what thanks actually is and where it comes from. Its five sessions look at why Scripture names ingratitude as the first turn away from God rather than a small failing; at eucharisteo, the word for giving thanks, and the meal the church named after it; at gratitude tested in plenty and in want, with the ten lepers and the difference between thanks "in" all circumstances and thanks "for" them; at gratitude and grief held together; and at the ordinary practices that slowly form a grateful heart.

It's built so a busy small group or a volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries notes on what it's after, and every session ends in prayer rather than in a performance of thankfulness.

One thing this study will never do is tell a grieving person to be grateful for the grave, or hand someone who is suffering a command to smile. Scripture asks for thanks in all circumstances, not for all of them. Gratitude in the Bible walks through grief rather than papering over it. Where there's real despair, the study keeps the way to help in plain view. Thanks was never a mood to fake. It's the recognition that a whole life is unearned, spoken to the One who gave it.
guides.audience: Small groups, individuals, and anyone learning to live grateful

guides.title: Grief: A Bible Study on Loss and the God Who Wept
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on grief, loss, lament, and a hope that doesn't pretend the pain away.
guides.blurb:
This study is for people who are grieving, for the small groups and grief groups that gather around them, and for anyone who loves someone in loss and doesn't know what to say. Its five sessions move slowly. They begin with Jesus at the grave of his friend Lazarus, weeping before he called him out. They give back the language of lament that fills the Psalms, Job, and Lamentations. They name death the way Paul names it, as an enemy. They set out a hope grounded in the resurrection of Jesus, one that doesn't ask anyone to stop crying. And they end with the comfort God gives becoming, in time, comfort we can give. A volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Each question comes with a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer.

The study won't hurry anyone toward closure. It won't tell a mourner that everything happens for a reason, or that time heals, or that God needed another angel, and it asks the leader not to let the room say those things either. It holds that death is real and wrong, that the resurrection is real and doesn't take the sting out of the grave in the meantime, and that a Christian may weep without shame and be angry without losing faith. Christians have written this way before. C. S. Lewis kept a notebook in the weeks after his wife died and published it as A Grief Observed, and Nicholas Wolterstorff wrote Lament for a Son after his son died in a climbing accident. This study keeps company with them, and with every person in the room who is still carrying someone.
guides.audience: People who are grieving, grief groups, and those who care for them

guides.title: Heaven and Hell: A Bible Study on the Life to Come
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on heaven, hell, and the life to come, and a hope that produces courage instead of escape.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who've grown tired of a hope that sounds like clouds and harps and have started to suspect the Bible promises something larger, stranger, and far more solid. Its five sessions clear away the wrong picture of heaven; recover the resurrection of the body and the renewal of creation, what N. T. Wright calls "life after life after death"; face hell honestly, setting out the traditional view of eternal conscious punishment, the conditionalist view, and universalism each at its strongest, with no gloating and no flinching; sit with what happens when we die and the communion of saints, holding grief and hope together at the graveside; and end where the faith ends, with how the coming morning shapes the long defeat we're living now. A busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question comes with a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer.

This study won't hand frightened people easy certainties, and it won't use hell as a whip. The doctrine of hell isn't comfortable, and the objections to it deserve to be heard at full weight. Most of us have at some point wanted to flee a world that breaks our hearts, or to give up on the horizon and call that wisdom. The study is written from inside that longing and doubt and grief, and the leader can lead from there too.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Hospitality: A Bible Study on the Open Door
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on hospitality, the stranger, and the table.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has mixed up hospitality with entertaining and wants to know what it really is, and for small groups and churches ready to practice it rather than admire it. Over five sessions it looks at the word Scripture uses, philoxenia, love of the stranger, which isn't the dinner party we give for people who will give one back. It sits with Abraham running to meet three strangers in the noon heat, and with the warning that some have welcomed angels without knowing it. It watches the table Jesus kept and the scandal of who he ate with. It looks at the early church as a household with an open door. And it ends where we live now, with the lonely neighbor across the hall, the immigrant family nobody wants, the outsider we'd rather not seat, and the real cost of leaving the door open. A busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation: every question carries notes for the leader, and every session ends in prayer.

This isn't a study that hands out tips for a nicer gathering. I know the habit it names from the inside: keeping the door shut, saving the table for people like us, treating a messy house as a good excuse and a busy week as a mercy to ourselves. The study turns down two easy ways out. One makes hospitality a performance staged in a beautiful home. The other hands the stranger to a program, so that no actual stranger ever crosses anyone's actual threshold. In Scripture, hospitality isn't a gift for the outgoing and the well-decorated. It's a command, and it rests on a God who set a table for his enemies and welcomed us while we were still strangers to him.
guides.audience: Individuals, families, and small groups; useful for churches rethinking welcome

guides.title: Identity: A Bible Study on Who You Actually Are
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on who you are: stepping out of the project of making yourself and into an identity given before it was ever performed.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and anyone worn out by the work of being themselves. Not the work of a hard job or a hard week, but the work of holding up a self you have to keep building, defending, updating, and selling, with no day off and no final version. It's for the person who did what our age told them to do, looked inward, found their "true self," became it, posted it, and still lies awake suspecting none of it is holding. And it's for the skeptic who has heard the church give a thin answer to the deepest question a person asks, "Who am I?", and walked away unconvinced. They deserve a better account than the one they got.

Our age handed everyone one instruction and called it freedom: look inward, find your true self, define yourself on your own terms, then become that self and present it to the world for approval. It sounds like liberation. For many it's become hard labor, being your own author and your own audience at once. These five sessions look at where that idea of the self came from, why it's so tiring, and the older answer it replaced: identity not as something you assemble but as a gift you receive. Not the self you make, but the self you're given.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Justice: A Bible Study on What the Bible Means by Justice
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on God, the poor, and the justice the church forgot.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and anyone tired of hearing the word justice used as a flag for one political team and a curse word by the other, while the widow still waits at the gate and nobody in the room can say what the Bible actually means by the word. It walks slowly through five movements drawn from James Bell's book Mishpat, on the two Hebrew words the prophets refuse to separate, on the way God leans toward the poor and the foreigner on every page, on the worship God said He hated because of the worker underneath it, on the dividing wall the cross already tore down and the faces with no voice at the gate, and on the systemic sin that outlives the sinner and the shape love finally takes when it reaches the place where the powerless wait.

This is not a study that smuggles a party platform into the church under cover of a Bible word. It will not do that, and the leader must not let it. It is also not a study that lets the comfortable keep a private, spiritual gospel that never once disturbs a balance sheet or a pew. It refuses both, on purpose, all the way through. Most of all it implicates the leader and the writer. Bell does not stand above this. Many of us have preached or heard righteousness as if it meant only a soul scrubbed clean, praised the Magnificat and gone home to lives arranged so we would never meet anyone Mary was singing about, used the basin to keep our own hands looking clean. He writes from inside that indictment. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Lament: A Bible Study on Praying Your Pain
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on suffering and lament, anchored in the Psalms and Job.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult classes, and anyone who has sat in a church that knew how to praise and didn't know what to do with someone who couldn't. Its five sessions are about suffering and a kind of prayer many churches have stopped praying. The first asks how lament went missing from our worship. The second learns the shape of the lament psalms from Psalm 13, which turns toward trust, and Psalm 88, which ends in the dark. The third sits with Job and the friends who explained too much. The fourth comes to the cross, where Jesus prayed a lament himself. The fifth looks for a hope that isn't denial. A volunteer can lead it with no preparation; each question comes with a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer.

The study won't hurry anyone out of grief or tell a suffering person that everything happens for a reason. In 1986 the Old Testament scholar Walter Brueggemann wrote about what he called the costly loss of lament: what a church gives up when it allows only praise. The Psalms gave Israel words for the dark, and Job's long protest is in the Bible, not edited out. This study takes both seriously, and it lets Psalm 88 end where it ends.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and anyone carrying a grief or a question they haven't been able to pray

guides.title: Lent: A Bible Study for the Forty Days
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study from Ash Wednesday to Holy Saturday on dust, the wilderness, returning to God, the way of the cross, and the darkest week.
guides.blurb:
Lent is the forty days before Easter, kept by many churches and not by others. This study is for a church or small group walking from Ash Wednesday to Easter, and for anyone who has never kept Lent and wonders why anyone would. Its first session begins where Ash Wednesday begins, with the sentence spoken to the first man, "For dust you are, and to dust you shall return" (Genesis 3:19), and with the psalm that says the LORD "is mindful that we are dust" (Psalm 103:14). The second follows Jesus into the wilderness, where he answered hunger and temptation with the words Moses spoke about the manna. The third hears Joel's call to return and prays Psalm 51 as David's confession, refusing the idea that repentance means punishing yourself. The fourth reads the call to take up the cross in Mark 8, beside Isaiah's suffering servant. The fifth walks through Mark 14 and 15 and ends where the women ended, at a sealed tomb on the Sabbath, with Easter morning still ahead. Each session is built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation beyond reading the leader's primer once.

The study doesn't settle whether Christians should keep Lent. Some churches receive the season as a gift from the early church; others hold that believers are free of any season Scripture doesn't command, and they have watched the custom harden into a law or turn into a show. Both are stated in their strongest form. Fasting comes with the health cautions first, and no one needs to fast from food to keep this study. Nor does the study stand outside its subject: the church has turned Lent into a diet with a religious label, a contest over who gave up the most, and a season of guilt, and it has also let fasting itself slip away and forgotten what it was for. No one leads this study from above either failure.
guides.audience: Churches and small groups keeping Lent, and anyone who has never kept it and wonders why anyone would

guides.title: Manhood: A Bible Study on What a Man Is For
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on masculinity, strength, and the man Jesus was.
guides.blurb:
This study is for men who are tired of being handed two masculinities and told to pick, the swaggering one that mistakes volume for strength and the soft one that mistakes absence for peace, and who suspect the truth is neither. It walks slowly through five sessions on what biblical manhood actually is once the culture-war caricatures are cleared away, on the father wound and the God who names himself Father of the fatherless, on strength under control in the man who wept and washed feet and drove the money changers out with a whip, on emotional honesty and friendship and the silence that is killing men who will not say they are drowning, and on servant leadership against domination, and the calling every man has to raise or mentor the next one. It is built so a busy man or a volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer rather than in the performance men so often bring into a room of other men.

This is not a study that stands over men and grades them. The writer came to faith out of atheism, was raised without a father, and is now raising five sons, and both of those last facts sit under every line. He does not write from a safe distance. Many of us have been the man who confused controlling a room with leading it, who went silent for days rather than say he was afraid, who reached for anger because it felt more like strength than the truth did. He writes from inside that indictment, and so will you. And it refuses both counterfeits with equal force. It will not baptize the domineering man who reads Scripture as a permit for his temper, and it will not excuse the passive man who calls his absence humility. It holds up one man as the measure, the one who had all the strength there is and bent it entirely toward the good of the people in front of him.
guides.audience: Men, fathers, sons, and the small groups and mentoring pairs that carry them

guides.title: Marriage: A Bible Study on Covenant Love
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on marriage as covenant, past the tips, into the cross.
guides.blurb:
This study is for married couples, engaged couples, and the small groups that carry them, people who are tired of marriage taught as a list of techniques and want to know what it actually is. Its five sessions take up covenant against contract; conflict and the long work of forgiveness; headship and submission read as mutual self-giving, never as a license to rule; sex and faithfulness; and money and in-laws, the real pressure points where vows get tested, ending with what it means to stay. A busy couple or a volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question comes with a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer, not in the argument a couple drove to group already having.

The study doesn't stand above marriage handing out advice. It's written toward the room where two people who love each other still hurt each other on a Tuesday over nothing. Many of us have been the spouse who kept a record we swore we'd forgiven, who confused leading with getting our way, who let a screen become the easier thing to turn toward. And there's one place this study will never go: it will never tell anyone that the covenant is a command to endure being harmed. Where there is abuse there is no covenant to keep, only a person to protect and a sin to name, and the study says so plainly and points toward safety and help (the National Domestic Violence Hotline, 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788; in immediate danger, call 911). The covenant pictures Christ laying down his life. It was never permission for one spouse to take another's.
guides.audience: Married couples, engaged couples, and small groups

guides.title: Mental Health: A Bible Study on the Weight You Carry
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on faith, the mind, and the God who meets the desperate.
guides.blurb:
This study is for the person carrying a weight they can't pray off, and for the small groups that want to sit with them without flinching or rushing to fix it. Its five sessions move slowly. They begin with the Bible's own plain speech about anguish, where a prophet lies under a tree and asks to die and isn't rebuked for it. They take apart the false choice the church keeps forcing between faith and therapy, and between trust and medication. They read Philippians 4 about anxiety, a thing the body suffers and not only a sin the soul commits. They name a depression that is a dark night and not a moral failure. And they end with the church as a place where the crushed are carried instead of shamed. A volunteer with no clinical training can lead it. Every question comes with a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer, never in a diagnosis nobody asked for.

There are two lines this study won't cross. It will never tell a suffering person that real illness is only weak faith, or that the answer to a mind that won't quiet is to pray harder or believe better. That's cruelty with a Bible in its hand. And it will never pretend that a small group can stand in for real help. Where there is danger, where a person is thinking of ending their life, the faithful thing is to get help now, and in the United States that means calling or texting 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, available every hour of every day. Therapy is a gift of God. So is medicine, and so is a good doctor. The God who made the body doesn't despise the mending of it, and neither will this study.
guides.audience: Anyone carrying anxiety, depression, or grief, and the small groups and pastors who walk with them

guides.title: Money, Work and the Poor: A Five-Session Bible Study
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study that refuses both the preacher who blesses your portfolio and the politics that swallows the gospel, and keeps the cross at the center of money.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who are tired of hearing money preached either as a blessing to claim or as a system to tear down, and who want to know what Scripture actually says. It walks through five of my essays: what the Bible says about money, whether poverty is political, the economy God commanded in the Jubilee, the eye of the needle, and the difference between charity and justice. A busy volunteer can lead it with little preparation. Every question carries the thinking behind it, and every session ends in prayer rather than argument.

It won't flatter one party and scold the other. It asks the Christian who has shrunk justice down to a check written on Tuesday whether he has built himself a hiding place, and it asks the Christian who has shrunk the gospel down to a voting bloc whether he still believes the cross can accomplish anything without a majority. Most of all it includes the leader, and it includes me. Most of us have reached for security a thousand times and called it prudence, lent and expected a return, and worn clothes made by hands we'll never meet. I'm writing from inside that, not above it, and I'll ask you to lead from there too.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Money: A Bible Study on Where Your Treasure Is
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on money, the heart, and the freedom Christ offers.
guides.blurb:
This is the small-group companion to James Bell's book Where Your Treasure Is, and it is not about the economy. It is about your heart and what it has quietly done with money. It walks slowly through five sessions on the heart that follows its treasure, the contentment we keep mistaking for resignation, the rich fool who confused a full barn with a safe soul, the anxiety that drives our reaching, and the strange freedom of the open hand. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Each question comes with a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer.

This is not a study that flatters the generous and indicts the greedy, because Bell does not believe the line runs there. It catches the man who gives and still grips, the woman who has little and still worships what she lacks, the giver who has used his giving to stop the question before it reached his heart. None of us stands outside this. Many of us have lain awake doing arithmetic we called prudence, felt our chests loosen at a number in an account and called the loosening peace, loved our children and let the love become a reason to reach for more and never enough. The question is never whether you may have money. The question is what your heart has done with it, and whether you can hear, under all the wanting, the voice of the One who became poor so that you could be free.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: New Believers: A Study on Your First Steps of Faith
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study for the brand new Christian, on what just happened and how to walk the long road that follows.
guides.blurb:
This study is for the person to whom something real has just happened, for the recently baptized still dripping and unsure what comes next, and for the seeker standing at the edge of it all, wondering what they would be signing up for. It walks slowly through five movements. What the new birth actually is and how a person can know it took. The Bible, what it is and how to read it without drowning on page one. Prayer, which is nothing more complicated than honest speech toward a Father who already knows. The church, the people you cannot follow Jesus without. And the long road, repentance and obedience and the slow reordering of an ordinary life over years. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every old church word gets defined on the spot rather than assumed.

This is not a study that hands a new believer a list of rules and tells them to perform. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. The thing that happened to these people happened by grace, which is the old word for love they did not earn and cannot pay back, and everything that follows runs on the same grace or it does not run at all. The study refuses two opposite errors. It refuses the cheap welcome that asks nothing and pretends following Jesus costs nothing, because it costs everything. And it refuses the heavy yoke that buries a new Christian under expectations before they have learned to stand, because that is how you crush a seedling. Most of all it implicates the writer. Bell came to faith from atheism. He knows what it is to stand outside the whole thing certain it was not true. He writes from inside the beginning, not above it. So will you.
guides.audience: New believers, the recently baptized, and seekers

guides.title: Parenting: A Bible Study on Forming a Child's Faith
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on parenting as formation, not performance, past the tips and into the cross.
guides.blurb:
This study is for parents, grandparents, and the small groups that carry them, who are tired of parenting taught as a set of techniques for producing an impressive child and want to know what the thing is actually for. It walks slowly through five sessions on formation against performance, on discipline that shapes a heart without dominating one, on a faith that cannot be handed down by force and the doubts a child must be allowed to own, on screens and attention and what a divided childhood does to a soul, and on the long and terrible mercy of letting go. It is built so a tired parent or a volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer rather than in the guilt a parent already drove to group carrying.

This is not a study that stands above parenting and dispenses advice. The writer came to faith from atheism and was raised without a father. He has five sons. He does not point from a safe distance. Many of us have been the parent who confused a child's performance with our own worth, who disciplined out of our own anger and called it correction, who tried to force a faith that can only be given, who let a screen become the easier thing to hand a child, who gripped a growing child too tightly out of our own fear. He writes from inside that indictment. So will you. And the one place this study will not go, ever, is to tell a parent that the shaping of a child is a license to break one. Where discipline has become domination, where correction has become harm, there is no formation happening, only a wound being passed down, and the study says so plainly and points toward help. The rod in Scripture images a God who disciplines the ones he loves for their good and never for his rage. It was never a permission to crush a child in the name of raising one.
guides.audience: Parents, grandparents, and small groups

guides.title: Pastoral Health: A Study for Leaders and Those Who Love Them
guides.eyebrow: A plainspoken five-session study on the exhaustion, hiddenness, and quiet despair of the people who shepherd us, for boards and leadership teams to read alongside the pastor they're trying to keep.
guides.blurb:
This study is for elder boards, deacon teams, leadership councils, and the spouses and friends who love a pastor and can see he's tired in a way that worries them. Its five sessions ask why faithful pastors leave, why so many are quietly depressed, how a man can lose his soul while building a church, why his hidden life is the first thing to starve, and why a church should require its pastor to rest. A busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question comes with a note for the leader, every session has a case to talk through, and every session ends in prayer rather than a plan.

It won't scold the pastor for being weak or the board for being blind. It asks something harder: that the leadership look at a way of doing church they helped build, one that can wear out the most faithful man in the room and then mourn him in real confusion about what went wrong. Read it with your own pastor in the room, or at least with his face in your mind.

A plain word before you begin. This material touches burnout, and in two sessions it touches clinical depression directly. Depression is not a failure of faith, and exhaustion is not a character flaw. Where a pastor is struggling with depression or any mental illness, the right and faithful step is a medical doctor and a licensed counselor, the same as for any other illness of the body. If a pastor is in crisis, call or text 988. Seeking help is an act of faith, not a confession of failure. There is no shame anywhere in this room.
guides.audience: Pastors, elder boards, and church leadership teams

guides.title: Prayer: A Bible Study on Learning to Pray
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on prayer, walking slowly through the words Jesus gave us.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and anyone who has been praying for years and quietly suspects they never learned how. It's also for people who stopped praying because the words ran out or the heavens went quiet. It walks through the prayer Jesus gave when his own disciples, who had watched him pray, asked him to teach them. It isn't a book about prayer. It's a school of prayer that runs on the words of the Lord's Prayer, one clause at a time.

The five sessions follow the prayer in order. Who we pray to, and how we dare to call him Father. What we're really asking when we ask for his name to be hallowed and his kingdom to come. The daily bread that ends our pretending we feed ourselves. The forgiveness we receive and the forgiveness we're then bound to give. And the prayer prayed in the dark, when the asking goes unanswered and the faithful thing left is to keep asking.

The study won't hand anyone a technique for getting God to perform, and the leader shouldn't either. Prayer isn't a lever. It's a child speaking to a Father, and some people in the room have no working picture of a father at all, because theirs left, or never came, or stayed and did harm. The study is written from inside the struggle with prayer, not from above it, and it asks the leader to lead from the same place.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Questions Skeptics Ask: A Study for Doubters
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study for skeptics and seekers asking whether Christianity is true.
guides.blurb:
This study is for the person who doesn't believe, or isn't sure, and is willing to look anyway. It's also for the friend who invited them, who is about to find out how much harder it is to defend the faith than to assume it. Nothing here is a trick. There's no emotional ambush waiting in session five, no moment when the lights dim and you're asked to decide something you didn't come to decide. Each session takes one hard question, states the strongest case against Christianity first, and only then offers a response, and the response is allowed to be incomplete.

The five questions come in order: whether anyone is there at all; whether science has buried God; who Jesus actually was; whether the resurrection happened; and what kind of step faith is if the evidence doesn't force it. Along the way the study names serious thinkers on both sides, including C. S. Lewis, Alvin Plantinga, N. T. Wright, David Hume and Bart Ehrman, not to end the conversation but because they've done the work and are worth reading. A host who isn't an expert can lead it, and should say "I don't know" when that's true. No question is ever met with shame. Someone who asks the hard thing out loud is doing something brave, and the room exists to make that safe.
guides.audience: Skeptics, seekers, agnostics, and the friends who invited them

guides.title: Raising Believers: A Bible Study for Christian Parents
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on passing a durable faith to children in a secular age.
guides.blurb:
This study is for parents, grandparents, and small groups of families who want their children to know God and who are quietly terrified that wanting it is not enough. It walks slowly through five movements drawn from James Bell's book Raising Believers, on what the home is actually for in the formation of faith, on teaching the next generation the way the Shema commands, on answering the hard questions children ask instead of flinching from them, on a faith built to survive doubt and the years away from home, and on the parenting of grace rather than the parenting of fear. It is built to be run by a tired parent with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than a parenting tip.

This is not a study that promises a method that guarantees believing children. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. Scripture is full of faithful parents whose children walked away, and the Bible itself records sons of godly men who wanted nothing to do with the God of their fathers. The home is the primary place where faith is handed on, and that is true and weighty and worth everything we have. But the home is not a machine that produces belief, and the gospel, not technique, is finally the hope of any child. The study holds both without flinching, and it refuses to sell parents a formula that will leave them crushed and self-blaming if a child wanders. Most of all it implicates the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He has five sons. Most parents have prayed over beds and not known if the prayers landed, answered a hard question badly and lain awake about it, parented from fear and called it diligence. He writes from inside the worry of a father who cannot save his own children and knows it. So will you.
guides.audience: Parents, grandparents, and small groups of families

guides.title: Sabbath: A Bible Study on Rest and Hurry
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on Sabbath, rest, and the God who stopped on the seventh day.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, Sunday school classes and individuals who are tired in a way sleep doesn't touch, who suspect their exhaustion isn't only a scheduling problem, and who feel a vague guilt about rest they can't quite name. Its five sessions move slowly: the God who rested when he didn't need to; rest as a refusal to be defined by what we produce; the Lord who said the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath; what a day of real rest looks like; and the rest that still remains for the people of God. Along the way it draws on Abraham Joshua Heschel's The Sabbath, Walter Brueggemann's Sabbath as Resistance, and Eugene Peterson. A volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Each question comes with a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

It won't hand anyone a tidy schedule and call it holiness. Sabbath can easily become one more thing to perform well, and this study refuses that.
