It also refuses the opposite idea, that rest is for the weak and serious Christians keep grinding. And it knows that for some people in some seasons, a whole day off really isn't possible. Most of us aren't in that position, though. Most of us simply don't stop, and this study asks why.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Singleness: A Bible Study for the Unmarried
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on singleness, calling, and belonging.
guides.blurb:
This study is for single people: the never-married, the widowed and the divorced, those who chose singleness and those who didn't. It's also for the small groups and churches that have too often left them standing in the lobby. Its five sessions take up singleness as a calling rather than a deficiency; desire and loneliness, which nobody should be shamed for feeling; chastity as honor for a body that is good; the church as a family wider than the nuclear household; and contentment and the fruit a single life can bear. A volunteer can lead it without preparation. Each question carries a note for the leader, and each session ends in prayer.

The church has largely been built around couples and families: the sermon series on marriage, the family potluck, the couples' small group. Single people have often been left to feel that the meeting hasn't started yet. I'm a pastor, and this study doesn't point at that from a safe distance; pastors built those churches. It lets the single voices of Scripture carry the weight: Jesus, Paul and Jeremiah. It won't treat singleness as a lesser Christianity or a holding pattern. It will honor the person content in it and sit beside the person aching in it, and it won't tell either one that they're half of something waiting to be completed.
guides.audience: Single adults, the widowed and divorced, and the churches and groups that carry them

guides.title: Spiritual Habits: A Bible Study on Formation
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on habits, desire, and the slow work of being formed.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has known the right thing and couldn't do it, who has filled the head with correct belief and watched the life go on unchanged, and for small groups tired of a discipleship that hands more information to people who already have plenty. Its five sessions take up an old truth the church nearly forgot: we're shaped less by what we think than by what we love, and love is trained by what we repeat. It looks plainly at the habits already forming us, the phone and the feed and the store, and asks what they're aiming the heart at. It recovers the historic spiritual disciplines as counter-formation. It refuses the false war between grace and effort. And it ends with a rule of life small enough that an ordinary person could keep it. It's built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries notes on what it's after, and every session ends in prayer.

Most of us live in the gap between the theology we could pass a test on and the people we actually are. I do. We assumed we'd be made holy by getting our thinking straight, and we weren't. So the one thing this study won't do is turn formation into a performance you put on to earn God's favor. The disciplines aren't the price of grace. They're how grace, already given, gets down into the muscles. We don't train to be loved. We train because we already are.
guides.audience: Individuals, small groups, and anyone tired of a faith that stays in the head

guides.title: Spiritual Warfare: A Bible Study on the Unseen Battle
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the powers, the armor of God, and the war we can't see.
guides.blurb:
This study is for Christians who suspect the New Testament means something real when it says our fight isn't against flesh and blood, and who are tired of choosing between two poor options: the church that finds a demon behind every bush and the church that has quietly stopped believing in the devil at all. Over five sessions it takes up the New Testament's picture of the powers, the armor of God read piece by piece, temptation and the enemy within, the victory Christ won at the cross, and the plain means by which ordinary Christians stand: prayer, Scripture, the gathered church and the Lord's Table. Every question carries a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer.

C. S. Lewis warned that there are two opposite mistakes we can make about the devils, disbelief and an unhealthy fascination, and that they're pleased by both. This study tries to live between those mistakes. It won't sell you a war story to thrill you, and it won't talk you out of a war the Scriptures plainly describe. The battle is real, the outcome is already decided, and the weapons handed to an ordinary believer are almost embarrassingly plain: a belt, a shield, a book, a prayer, a shared loaf.
guides.audience: Christians, small groups, and anyone unsure what to make of the New Testament's language about the powers

guides.title: Suffering: A Bible Study for When Life Does Not Make Sense
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on suffering, lament, and the God who doesn't explain but comes.
guides.blurb:
This study is for people in pain, for the people sitting near them who have run out of things to say, and for small groups willing to hold a hard question without rushing to close it. Its five sessions take the problem of pain at its full weight through Job; recover lament as faithful speech through the Psalms; come to the cross, where God answered suffering by entering it rather than explaining it; look at Paul's thorn and the grace that was enough when the thorn stayed; and end with the new creation, where God himself wipes away every tear. A volunteer can lead it with no training. Each question comes with a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer.

It refuses the sentences the church reaches for when it's uncomfortable, like "everything happens for a reason" and "God needed another angel," and it refuses just as firmly the despair that reads a wound as proof no one is there. It won't tell a person in agony that the answer is to trust more, or that their grief is a failure of faith. Where the pain has turned toward self-harm or despair that will not lift, the study says plainly that this is the moment to reach for a pastor, a counselor, a doctor, or a crisis line (in the US, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline), and to reach today. The gospel doesn't require anyone to suffer alone. The God at the center of this study wept at a grave he was about to open.
guides.audience: Anyone in grief or pain, those walking with them, and small groups

guides.title: The Beatitudes: A Bible Study on the Kingdom of God
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the Beatitudes and the kingdom Jesus announced.
guides.blurb:
This study is for Christians, seekers and the small groups that carry them, people who have heard the Beatitudes read at funerals and seen them printed on wall art and never quite felt their edge. Over five sessions it walks through the eight sayings Jesus spoke on a hillside in Galilee: first the word "blessed" itself, and the strange fact that Jesus speaks it over exactly the people the world counts as losing; then the poor in spirit and those who mourn, the meek and the hungry, the merciful and the pure in heart, the peacemakers and the persecuted. Every question carries a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer.

One conviction runs through all five weeks. The Beatitudes describe before they demand. They are a verdict God speaks over unlikely people before they are a picture of the life grace grows in them, and never a ladder anyone has to climb to get in. Read the other way, they become the heaviest law ever laid on a human back. Read in their own order, they are a door held open to people who assumed they were shut out.
guides.audience: Christians, seekers, and small groups

guides.title: The Church and Political Power Through History: A Five-Session Study
guides.eyebrow: A pastoral five-session study on how the church has lived with political power, from a coin held up to trap Jesus to the end of Christendom, keeping the crucified King above every throne.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult classes, and anyone who feels the ground shifting under the faith in their country and wants to know what is actually dying and what isn't. It works through five of my essays on the long marriage of church and empire: the coin held up to trap Jesus, the three centuries the church grew with no power at all, the teaching of two kingdoms, and the slow end of the arrangement that made Christianity the default religion of the West. It explains the hard words plainly and never sneers at the believer who grieves the change. A busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer rather than argument.

It doesn't flatter the people who want to seize the culture or the people who want to flee it. It asks the Christian reaching for the levers of the state whether he has mistaken a borrowed majority for the work of the Spirit, and it asks the Christian who has washed his hands of public life whether he has called retreat holiness. I'm not outside this either. I've heard the render line preached as a permission slip, I've seen flags stand on platforms no one would move, and part of me misses the store that closed on Sunday.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The Church: A Bible Study on Why We Still Need Each Other
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the church, the body of Christ, and the call to belong to a people who will let you down.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult classes, and anyone who has loved the church and been hurt by it in roughly equal measure, which is most people who have stayed long enough to know it well. It moves through five sessions: what the church actually is; the life together Dietrich Bonhoeffer described from inside a community the Nazi state would scatter; the marks and the mess of a church that is a hospital for sinners rather than a museum for saints; the church sent into a culture that no longer assumes the faith; and the hard grace of committing to a flawed congregation instead of leaving the moment it proves flawed. Every question comes with a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer rather than a tidy resolution.

This study doesn't defend the church by pretending it's fine. The church has covered up abuse, baptized politics, preached to please its donors, and bored a watching world. We take all of that seriously. But the study also refuses the easy exit, the idea that the answer to a hypocritical church is no church and that a Christian can follow Jesus alone with a podcast and a Bible app. The New Testament doesn't know that Christian. I'm a pastor, I've failed the church in my own ways, and I love her anyway, the way you love a family you can't disown. I'm writing from inside the body, and I'm asking you to lead it that way.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The Creeds: A Bible Study on What Christians Believe
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the creeds and the faith settled before we arrived.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has said "I believe in God the Father Almighty" and never asked where the words came from or what they cost, and for groups that want to know the faith they inherited rather than one they put together by feel. It moves through five sessions. We start with the crisis that forced the church to write anything down: the fight over whether Jesus is God or the highest of God's creatures. Then we walk the Apostles' Creed line by line, sit with the one Greek word the council at Nicaea wouldn't give up, follow the harder argument at Chalcedon about how Jesus is fully God and fully human, and end by asking why saying an old creed out loud still forms a person who didn't write it. A volunteer with no background in church history can lead it. Every question carries a note for the leader, every date can be checked, and every session ends in prayer rather than a theological argument.

The word creed can sound like a loyalty oath, a wall built to keep thinking people out. Many people assume real faith is the private, wordless kind and that anything bishops wrote down in the fourth century is the dead part. This study takes that suspicion seriously and then shows why it's mistaken. It also refuses to treat the person who can't yet say the creed as a problem to be fixed. Doubt is welcome in the room. Saying words you aren't sure of yet isn't hypocrisy; it's often the first step, the way a person says a vow before feeling its whole weight. The creed isn't a test you pass to belong. It's the faith the church has held for two thousand years, held out to you, including on the days you can't hold it yourself.
guides.audience: New believers, lifelong churchgoers, skeptics, and small groups

guides.title: The End Times: A Bible Study on How the Story Ends
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the last things, holding open hands on the timeline and a closed fist on the center.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who are tired of being handed a chart and told it's the gospel. It's for the believer who has watched a predicted date come and go, who has seen a church split over the rapture, who has read Revelation and come away more confused than comforted, and who suspects there's more here than a code to crack. It moves through five subjects: how to read apocalyptic writing without turning it into a newspaper, the three readings of the thousand years, the rapture and the dispensational debate, the "already and not yet" every serious Christian shares, and the new creation that is the actual hope, the world made right rather than abandoned.

One rule governs the study. Every major view of the end is stated as its best advocates would state it, at full strength, before anyone argues against it. Premillennialism, postmillennialism, and amillennialism each get their best scholars and their strongest case from Scripture. The dispensational rapture gets Darby, Scofield, and Blaising at full strength before the alternatives answer. Faithful, careful, Bible-loving Christians have landed in all three camps for centuries, and a study that flattened them into one would be misleading you about the church.

What the study won't bend on is the center, and the leader has to guard it. Christ has come. Christ will come again. The dead will be raised. The world will be made right. On that there's no open hand. The timeline is where the room is free to disagree; the creed is where it isn't. And I'm inside this with you. I've felt the pull of date-math in the dark, and of treating the end as an escape from a world we're supposed to love.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The Fruit of the Spirit: A Bible Study on Growth
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the fruit of the Spirit and the life it forms, past the willpower, into the vine.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone worn out from trying to become a better person by force, and for small groups full of people who have quietly given up on it. Its five sessions walk slowly through the fruit of the Spirit Paul names in Galatians 5: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. It starts where Paul starts, with the difference between fruit that's grown and a work that's manufactured. Paul lists the works of the flesh in the plural, a scattered mess we produce ourselves, and he names the fruit in the singular, one harvest the Spirit grows in us.

That reading rules out the two mistakes that spoil most teaching on this passage. One treats the nine as a to-do list to grind out by willpower. The other treats them as a mood that arrives on its own while we wait. The study ends where Paul ends, in the war between the flesh and the Spirit, with the fruit real and the harvest not yet finished.

Most of us have spent years trying to produce the fruit by effort: gritting our teeth toward patience, performing a kindness we didn't feel, and calling the performance growth. I know that exhaustion from the inside, and this study is written from there. The one thing it won't do is hand a heavier list to people already crushed by striving. Our part is to stay rooted where the fruit grows, to abide in the vine and keep in step with the Spirit, and to stop pretending we can produce from ourselves what only God can grow.
guides.audience: Christians, new believers, skeptics of easy religion, and small groups

guides.title: The Holy Spirit: A Bible Study on the Forgotten God
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the Holy Spirit, the personal presence of God who gives life.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult classes and individuals who have spent years in church and somehow ended up with two persons of the Trinity they could describe and a third they couldn't. The Father they can picture. The Son they love. The Spirit has been left a kind of holy vapor, a power source, the part of God you mention at the end of a prayer and then forget. That isn't a small mistake. It's losing sight of God himself, present, personal and living in his people, the breath by which the dead are made alive.

The five sessions take up who the Spirit is and why we treat him as an afterthought; the new birth, in which the Spirit raises the spiritually dead and does what argument never could; the slow growth of his fruit, and the difference between being changed and performing; the contested question of the gifts, where continuationists and cessationists are both given their strongest case and the group is held together across the divide; and the Spirit in our weakness, who prays in us when we have no words and is the down payment of a world being made new.

This study won't pick the group's side in the old arguments over tongues, prophecy and healing, and no leader should let it. Each case is set out at full strength, and the aim is a room that can disagree about the gifts while worshiping the same Spirit. None of us stands outside what this study names. I don't, and neither will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The Image of God: A Bible Study on Human Worth
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the imago Dei and the dignity it gives every person.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has wondered what a human being is worth, and why, and who is tired of hearing the answer either puffed up into flattery or shrunk down to chemistry. It moves through five sessions on the oldest and boldest thing the Bible says about people: they're made in the image of God. We start in Genesis 1, with a sentence that sounded closer to sedition than to compliment in the world that first heard it, because the empires around Israel kept the divine image in the palace and Genesis gave it to everyone. Then we look at the three classic accounts of what the image is, and why that argument decides who gets counted as fully human. We face the fall, where the image was defaced but never erased. We follow the doctrine to Christ, who is the image of God, and into whose likeness the broken image is being remade. And we end in the street, with the poor, the unborn, the enemy, the stranger and the person who gets on your nerves, each one carrying a worth you didn't assign and can't revoke.

This isn't a study that admires human dignity from a safe height. Most of us assign worth on a sliding scale, generous to the useful and stingy toward the inconvenient, and I'm no exception. The doctrine of the image won't let you look down on a single human being without looking up into the face of the God who made them, and the people we find easiest to despise turn out to be the ones it was written to protect.
guides.audience: Adults, small groups, and anyone wrestling with human worth and dignity

guides.title: The Lord's Prayer: A Bible Study Line by Line
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the Lord's Prayer, line by line, past the recitation and into the words.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has said the Lord's Prayer a thousand times and stopped hearing it, for the small group that wants to learn to pray and doesn't know where to begin, and for the skeptic who suspects the whole thing is a formula recited on autopilot. It moves slowly through five sessions, one for each movement of the prayer Jesus taught when his disciples asked him how to pray. We start with the address, "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name," and refuse to let either the closeness or the awe swallow the other. We take the two petitions that pray against our own preferences, "your kingdom come, your will be done," and ask what it costs to mean them. We find dependence and enough in the request for daily bread. We face the small, hard word as in "forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors." And we end where the prayer ends, with "lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil," and the kingdom and the power and the glory that were never ours. A volunteer can lead it with little preparation: every question carries notes for the leader, and every session ends by praying the line it studied.

This isn't a study that stands above prayer and hands out technique. Many of us have prayed with our mouths while our minds wandered to the calendar, said "Our Father" for years before the word meant anything, and asked God to forgive us in the same breath we refused to forgive someone else. I have. And the one thing this study won't do is turn the Lord's Prayer into a method for getting what we want from God. Most of the prayer is about God's name, kingdom and will before it ever mentions our bread, and the whole of it is built to make us smaller and God larger, which is the opposite of what we usually come to prayer hoping to arrange.
guides.audience: New believers, seasoned Christians, seekers, and small groups learning to pray

guides.title: The Parables: A Bible Study on the Stories of Jesus
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the parables and the kingdom they hide and reveal.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has heard the parables so often they've stopped hearing them, and for small groups willing to be caught by the stories rather than only informed by them. It moves through five sessions: why Jesus taught in parables at all, a form built to reveal and conceal at once; the two lost sons of Luke 15 and the father who runs toward both; the good Samaritan and the question a lawyer used to protect himself; the kingdom parables of the mustard seed, the leaven, the hidden treasure and the sower, and the strange smallness of how God works; and the parables of grace and judgment, the vineyard workers, the unforgiving servant, and the sheep and the goats. A volunteer can lead it with little preparation: every question carries notes for the leader, and every session ends in prayer.

This isn't a study that stands above the parables and hands out their meaning. I read these stories without exempting myself from any of their wrong characters: the older brother keeping his ledger, the priest crossing the road, the servant forgiven a fortune and choking a neighbor over a hundred denarii. The parables were never illustrations that made hard truths easy. They were built to get past the guard a plain command would trip, and to let a hearer judge himself before he knew he was the one on trial. Read them expecting to be caught.
guides.audience: Small groups, Sunday classes, and any reader willing to be caught by a story

guides.title: The Psalms: A Bible Study on Honest Prayer
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the Psalms and the prayers we were afraid to pray.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has stood in church singing about God's goodness while something inside them was screaming, and for the small groups that carry those people. It walks slowly through five sessions on the Psalter as the church's prayer book, on the lament that God does not merely permit but invites, on the imprecatory psalms and what to do with the rage they voice, on the psalms of trust and thanksgiving that are earned and not pasted on, and on the psalms of ascent and the long climb of worship. It is built so a busy person or a volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer, because a study of the prayer book ought to teach a room to pray.

This is not a study that stands above the Psalms and admires them from a safe distance. The writer came to faith out of atheism. He was raised without a father, and he has five sons. He does not point from outside the Psalter. He writes as one still learning to pray it. And the one thing this study will not do is teach anyone that faith means presenting God with a cleaned-up face. The Psalms do the opposite. They put the rage, the grief, the doubt, and the terror into the mouth of the worshiper and call it prayer. A God who inspired Psalm 88 is not a God who needs to be protected from your honesty. He wrote the honest prayers first.
guides.audience: Believers, doubters, and small groups learning to pray

guides.title: The Resurrection: A Bible Study on the Evidence
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study weighing the historical case for the resurrection of Jesus, written for the skeptic.
guides.blurb:
This study is for the person who has decided the resurrection is a beautiful story and nothing more, for the Christian who has never heard anything to say to that person beyond "believe harder," and for the leader willing to host a room where both can speak freely. It takes the central claim of the Christian faith to the place it's most often dismissed, the question of whether it happened, and it doesn't treat the question as rude. It's the most important question there is. If a man was dead and then wasn't, everything changes. If he wasn't, Paul said our faith is futile, and he said it before any skeptic did (1 Corinthians 15:17).

The five sessions move in order. First, what the first Christians actually claimed and what they staked on it. Second, the short list of facts that most historians grant, believing or not. Third, the natural explanations, each put at its strongest and then tested. Fourth, the awkward detail of the women at the tomb. Fifth, what it would mean if it's true.

No study can hand anyone certainty in a box. History doesn't deal in proofs, only in probabilities weighed with care. What this one offers is a case strong enough that a thinking person can rest some weight on it without giving up their mind, and a room where nobody will be pushed to decide before they're ready.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, skeptics, and seekers

guides.title: The Sermon on the Mount: A Bible Study
guides.eyebrow: A six-session study on Matthew 5 to 7 and the kingdom it describes.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes and individuals who've heard the Sermon on the Mount preached as a set of lovely ideals nobody is expected to keep, or as a handful of sayings cut loose from the kingdom that gives them their weight. Its six sessions walk slowly through Matthew 5 to 7: the Beatitudes and the upside-down kingdom they announce; salt, light and the law Jesus drives down into the heart; the love of enemies; treasure, money and worry; judging, asking and the narrow gate; and the two houses and the storm. A volunteer can lead it without preparation. Each question carries a note for the leader, and each session ends in prayer rather than advice.

It won't let the sermon go soft. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, who wrote about this sermon in the 1930s for a church that had made grace cheap, put the cost plainly: "When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die." The Sermon on the Mount may be the most quoted and least obeyed teaching there is, and this study lives in the gap between the quoting and the obeying. It refuses two easy ways out. One files the sermon away as an ideal for some other world. The other turns it into rules we keep by trying harder. Both miss the grace it starts with and the obedience it ends with. And it doesn't stand on the mountain looking down. Most of us know the anger we've called principle and the money we've called stewardship, and I'm among them.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The Story of the Bible: A Study of the Whole Canon
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the Bible as a single story, from creation to new creation.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has read the Bible in pieces and suspected it was meant to be read whole, for skeptics who dismissed it as a grab bag of ancient rules and comforting verses, for Christians who know the parts but have never seen the shape, and for the small groups that carry both. It walks slowly through five sessions that follow the one story from its first line to its last, creation and the world made good, the fall and the long unraveling, Israel and the covenant people through whom God kept his word, Christ and the turning of the whole thing, and new creation, heaven come down to a healed earth. It borrows N. T. Wright's picture of a play in five acts, and the older frame of creation, fall, redemption, and restoration, not as a clever device but because the Bible tells itself that way and we forgot how to listen. It is built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer.

This is not a study that stands above the Bible and grades it. The writer came to faith from atheism, and he knows how most skeptics read Scripture, as disconnected fragments a person quotes to win an argument, a verse for weddings and a verse for funerals and a verse for whatever you already wanted to do. The skeptic is not wrong that the fragments, cut loose, can be made to say almost anything. He is wrong that fragments are all there is. What he cannot see, and what this study is built to help a person see, is that the sixty-six books are not a filing cabinet of religious sayings but a single, unfolding story with a beginning that explains the ache and an ending that answers it, and a center, a cross, that holds the whole arc together. Read that way, the Bible stops being a rulebook you obey or reject and becomes a story you find yourself inside. And once you are inside it, the question is no longer whether the verses are useful. The question is whether the story is true, and if it is, what it means that you were written into it before you ever picked up the book.
guides.audience: Skeptics, new believers, longtime Christians, and small groups

guides.title: The Trinity: A Bible Study on Knowing God
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the God who is three-in-one, and the life that knowing him makes possible.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult classes and individuals who have studied God for years and quietly suspect they've never met him, and for anyone who came to church looking for something to believe and found a doctrine called the Trinity that sounded like a math problem no one could solve. It walks through the oldest confession the church holds, that the one God is eternally three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and asks the question underneath all theology: was the point ever just to be right about God, or to know him?

The first session takes up the difference between knowing about God and knowing him, and the danger of theology that never becomes prayer. The second states the doctrine of the Trinity carefully and historically, not as a puzzle to crack but as the reason God can be called love. The third meets the Father who runs toward the returning child. The fourth looks at the Son, "the exact imprint" of God's nature, in whom the God who could have stayed unknown made himself known. And the fifth turns to the Spirit, who doesn't leave us studying God from across a room but draws us into the love the Father and the Son have always shared.

This study won't hand anyone a diagram of God to file away, and no leader should try. The Trinity isn't a problem to be solved. It's the name of the God who saves us, and Jesus said that knowing him is eternal life. Some in the room have spent years gathering facts about God and have never been sure they were known by him. I'm writing from inside that same long walk, from knowing about God toward knowing him.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: When Our Parents Grow Old: A Bible Study for Caregivers
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on honor, weariness, hard choices, and dying well, for those caring for an aging parent or an ailing husband or wife.
guides.blurb:
This study is for adult children caring for aging parents, near or far, for husbands and wives caring for a spouse whose body or mind is failing, and for the churches that should not leave them alone. Its five sessions take up what the command to honor father and mother asks of grown children; the weariness no one sees, with Elijah under the broom tree; the reversal of roles, through Ruth and Naomi and Jesus entrusting his mother to the disciple he loved; the hard choices about where a parent will live, money, siblings, and a parent who was not a good parent; and dying well and grieving, with a plain account of hospice and palliative care. Each session is built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation, and each ends in prayer rather than advice.

This guide is not medical, legal, or financial advice. It says plainly that caregiver exhaustion and depression are real, that elder abuse and neglect happen, sometimes at the hands of family, and that safety comes first. A caregiver with thoughts of suicide should call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, now. So should a caregiver afraid of hurting the person they care for, after making sure that person is safe and stepping away; no one has to be suicidal to call. Anyone who suspects an older adult is being harmed, neglected, or exploited should report it to adult protective services, and call 911 if anyone is in danger.

The study refuses two easy answers: that honor means doing it all yourself, and that grown children owe their parents only what they choose to give. Scripture commands honor as something weighty and done in deeds, sets rest beside it, and gives the burden to a family and a church rather than to one exhausted son or daughter. Where faithful Christians differ, the study states each view fairly and leaves the question open. And it implicates the church, which has too often prayed for the sick by name and forgotten the people who bathe them.
guides.audience: Adult children caring for aging parents, spouses caring for a husband or wife, and the churches around them

guides.title: Where Is God When It Hurts: Suffering and the Goodness of God
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the problem of evil, the providence of God, and the hope that does not disappoint.
guides.blurb:
This study is for the person who has stood at a hospital bed, or a graveside, or in the wreckage of a marriage or a diagnosis, and asked the oldest question there is. If God is good, and God is able, why this. It is for the skeptic who left the faith over a child's cancer ward and was never given an answer worth the name, and for the Christian still inside the faith carrying a question the church kept handing them platitudes for. It is for the pastor who has run out of things to say at funerals. It does not promise to solve the problem of evil, because no honest book ever has, and the ones that pretend to are the ones that wound. It promises something harder and more durable. It takes the objection at its full and terrible strength, refuses every cheap answer, and walks toward the only response Scripture finally gives, which is not an argument but a Person who entered the suffering himself.

The five sessions move in order. First the question stated without flinching, the way the honest atheist states it, so well that the believer in the room feels it too. Then the doctrine of providence held without tidy resolution, a God who permits what he hates and works it toward an end we cannot see from inside it. Then the book of Job, where God answers the sufferer not with an explanation but with a whirlwind and a thousand questions, and rebukes the friends who had the formula. Then the cross, where the God who permits suffering does not stay outside it but enters it, bleeds inside it, dies inside it. And finally the hope that does not explain suffering away but defeats it, the resurrection and the new creation where every tear is wiped from every face. Bell does not write this from a safe distance. He came to God from atheism, and he does not pretend the problem of evil is a small wall. He is not solving a puzzle for you. He is standing in the rubble with you, pointing at the only light the dark could not put out.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Who Am I, Really? A Bible Study for Teenagers
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study for students on identity, the phone, anxiety, friendship, and a faith they can call their own.
guides.blurb:
This study is for students roughly thirteen to eighteen, for the youth groups and classes that gather them, and for the parents, grandparents, and leaders who love them. It walks through five questions teenagers are already asking, whether or not anyone at church has asked them out loud: who gets to say who I am, what the phone in my pocket is doing to me, what to do when I'm anxious, how to find real friends and a place to belong, and how a faith I was handed can become my own. Each session starts where students actually live, goes underneath to Scripture and the long memory of the church, and arrives at a way of seeing they can carry into rooms the study never mentions. It is built so a volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every discussion question carries the answer behind it, every quiet room has a backup question, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

The study takes teenagers seriously. It doesn't talk down to them, it doesn't treat them as a problem to be managed, and it doesn't pretend the adults have these things figured out. Most of the pressures it names, the performing, the screens, the worry, the loneliness, the borrowed faith, are things adults handed to young people or modeled in front of them, and the study says so. It is careful, too. Discussion questions invite and never require, no student is pressed to share anything private, and the leader primer tells leaders exactly what to do if a student discloses danger at home or thoughts of self-harm. Parents can read every word their students read.

LiveWell is the work of James Bell, a pastor who came to faith from atheism, was raised without a father, and has five sons. The conviction under every session is simple: the God who made you has spoken first, and his word about you is truer than any other.
guides.audience: Students roughly 13 to 18, youth groups, and the parents and leaders who love them

guides.title: Work and Vocation: A Bible Study on Faith and Your Job
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on work and vocation, and the faith that has to survive Monday.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and anyone who has sat in a pew on Sunday feeling that their faith was real and large, and then walked into a job on Monday where it seemed to shrink to nothing. It is for the believer who suspects, somewhere underneath, that the real work of God happens on a stage with a microphone and that their own forty hours at a desk or a register or a job site are spiritually beside the point. It walks slowly through five movements on what work is and was meant to be, on Eden where God himself worked and called it good, on the thorns and the sweat that came after, on the lie that splits the world into sacred jobs and secular ones, on the idol that work becomes when it stops being what we do and starts being who we are, and on the strange promise that our labor is not finally lost. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This is not a study that will tell you to find your passion and the rest will take care of itself, because most work is not passion and most weeks are not inspired, and the gospel has something to say to the ordinary Tuesday and not only to the calling that thrills you. It refuses two lies at once. The first says ordinary work does not matter to God, that only ministry counts, and the study takes that lie apart with Luther and Dorothy Sayers and the whole doctrine of vocation. The second says work is everything, the place we earn our worth and prove we exist, and the study names that as the idol it is. Most of all the study implicates the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He is a pastor, and the pastorate is a job, a job that can be loved into an idol, hidden behind, its busyness called faithfulness when it is really fear, the work of God made a way of avoiding God. He writes from inside the problem. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals
